#: protection collector: three kinds of document read as files — the rendered declaration, the hourly staleness verdict, and one receipt per job per outcome. Every payload is the (document, why-not) PAIR the adapter's module-level _load returns, so every path below is prefixed by the list index `*`, and the bare `*` entry is the why-not member itself.
#authored: The committed variant is AUTHORED, not captured, so no value here has ever been substituted and the run over it reports zero. That is not a reason to classify loosely — it is the reason to classify carefully. A real estate publishing these documents WAS captured on 2026-08-19 and deliberately not committed, and this manifest is what makes the next such capture safe by default rather than safe by somebody remembering. Every entry below is written for that capture, not for the invented one beside it.
#the-real-bound: Read this before adding a captured variant. `immutability` and `pruneAuthority` are security prose an operator WROTE, carried verbatim by the collection because paraphrasing a security property would be inventing a new claim. Verbatim prose about a private estate's off-site posture is the single least publishable thing these documents hold, and `prose` substitutes tokens inside it without making the sentence publishable. A capture from a real host is refused on judgement, not on this manifest — the classifications below let it be SCRUBBED, they do not make it publishable, and those are different questions.
#names: Three kinds of name run through these documents and they are not interchangeable. HOST names (`host`, `ownerHost`, and the host half of an implementedBy reference) locate a machine. TARGET, DESTINATION and JOB names are words an operator chose for what they protect and where it lands — `media-photos`, `offsite-critical` — and they disclose content rather than location: a reader learns what is worth backing up. Job names routinely EMBED a host name (`silo-appdata`), which is why they cannot be classified as opaque identifiers.
#keys-are-data: The dict keys under `targets` and `destinations` ARE the names above, and so are the keys under `implementedBy`, `implementedExternally` and `lastProvenAt` — the latter three being destination names. They are classified by ~key entries rather than by their values' paths, because a `*` in a path matches a key without classifying it.
#numbers: `schema`, the three `counts`, `ageSeconds`, `maxAgeSeconds`, `finishedAtEpoch` and `checkedAt` are `nothing`. The ages are durations, the counts are cardinalities of a set whose members are classified above, and the two epochs say when a job ran on a host nobody can name once the names are substituted.
#vocabularies: `state`, `basis`, `lastResult`, `result`, `exitStatus`, `class`, `kind`, `retention` and `cadence` are closed vocabularies the estate's own tooling writes — ok/stale, last-success/registered-never-succeeded, success/exit-code, backup/replicate/recreate. They are `nothing`: none is a word chosen per install, and substituting one would destroy the distinction every rule in rules/protection.py turns on.
#unit: A systemd unit name, and it embeds the job name — `protect-media-photos.service` — so it is classified with the same class as a job name and the `unit_name` ENCODING, which folds systemd's escaping before the pass runs and restores it after. Classifying it as a bare name would leave an escaped spelling of an operator's word untouched.
#why-not: The bare `*` is _load's second member: null when the file was read or absent, and the exception text when it would not open. That text carries a PATH — the receipt it failed on — so it takes the free-text pass rather than `nothing`.
